title: EF Core & Dapper
html:
EF Core & Dapper

Two ways to reach a relational database from .NET, suited to different jobs. Mixing them in one project is reasonable; mixing them in one operation is usually not.

EF Core

An object-relational mapper with change tracking. You query with LINQ, it produces SQL, and it remembers what it loaded so SaveChanges can work out the updates.

Change tracking is the feature and the cost. Loading entities you only intend to read still pays for snapshots and identity management. AsNoTracking on read-only queries is the single easiest win in most codebases.

Deferred execution. A LINQ query is not run until enumerated. That is what lets you compose it - and what makes ToList() in the middle of a chain expensive, because everything after it runs in memory over the whole table.

Client evaluation. If part of your expression cannot be translated, older versions silently ran it in memory. Current versions throw instead, which is far better: a query that cannot be translated is a query whose cost you did not choose.

The N+1 problem. Loading a list and then touching a navigation property per item issues one query per row. Fix with Include for a join, or a projection that fetches exactly the columns needed. This is the single most common performance defect in ORM code, and it does not show up until the list is long.

Projections. Select into a DTO and only those columns are fetched, with no tracking overhead. This is both the fastest read path and the right API boundary - returning entities couples your contract to your schema.

Migrations. Schema changes as versioned, scripted, reviewable code. Never edit one that has been applied anywhere. Check the generated SQL for anything destructive before running it.

Dapper

A thin mapper: you write the SQL, it fills objects. No tracking, no translation, nothing between you and the plan.

Right when the query is the point - reporting, complex joins, anything where you want to control the SQL exactly, or where the ORM's translation is fighting you.

Keep the SQL in named constants or dedicated files rather than inline in a method, so it can be found, reviewed and tested. And parameterise everything, always.

Choosing

Want Reach for
CRUD over an aggregate, with change tracking EF Core
A read model shaped for a screen EF Core projection, or Dapper
A gnarly report with window functions and CTEs Dapper
Bulk insert of many rows a bulk-copy API, not either
Full control of the execution plan Dapper

Pick one as the project's default and treat the other as the documented exception. Two ORMs used interchangeably means two sets of habits and two places to look.

Common mistakes

  • No AsNoTracking on read paths.
  • Lazy loading left on in a request path, producing N+1 queries invisibly.
  • Returning entities from an API, so a schema change breaks clients.
  • A DbContext used concurrently. It is not thread-safe; one per unit of work.
  • Filtering after projecting, when the filter could have run in the database.
  • Row-by-row inserts in a loop where a set-based statement or bulk copy would do.
